newsitem.title: USA: U.S. shuttle to come home on time.
newsitem.headline: U.S. shuttle to come home on time.

text.p: After a successful test of a troublesome space treadmill on Monday, NASA officials cleared the shuttle Atlantis for an on-time landing to bring home astronaut John Blaha.

Atlantis, which spent five days berthed at the Russian Mir space station, was set to land as originally scheduled at 7:48 a.m. EST (1248 GMT) on Wednesday. NASA managers had considered keeping it up an extra day if necessary to get crucial data on the performance of a treadmill destined for use on the future international space station.

The astronauts tested the treadmill last week but a laptop computer that monitored the device failed to record any data. Officials were not sure a repeat test squeezed into the flight plan could be completed in time, but the test appeared to go well and NASA decided to bring Atlantis home on time.
"Since all the (treadmill) activities have been completed there are no plans to extend the mission," mission operations director Bob Castle told a news conference.

Astronauts who spend long periods in space depend on exercise machines to keep their bones and muscles from wasting away, but the vibrations from exercise can ruin sensitive microgravity experiments. Three astronauts ran on the sophisticated treadmill designed to get around that problem, which appears to float in midair like a magic carpet.

The test was run after Atlantis pulled away from Mir on Sunday night after dropping off astronaut Jerry Linenger for a four-month stay in space. The shuttle was to return to Earth with Blaha, who had lived and worked aboard the Russian space station since September.

Blaha said was looking forward to being reunited with Brenda, his wife of 30 years. His mother Frances will also be at the landing site to greet him and planned to prepare the 54-year-old astronaut's favourite Mexican dish.

Blaha will have spent 128 days in space, the second longest space flight by an American. Shannon Lucid, his predecessor on Mir, currently holds the U.S. record for the longest aloft. She spent 188 days in space.
